finding.claim: The user identity is read directly from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified. Nothing in this code authenticates it, for example by checking a session, signature or token, or by confirming that a trusted proxy set it. Any caller can send the header with the name of a user who holds grants and be treated as that user. This bypasses the ACL checks on delete and rename. It is only safe if an upstream proxy always strips and re-sets this header, and that is not enforced or documented here.
finding.source: The attacker-controlled HTTP header X-Session-User-Verified on any request.
finding.sink: The protected operations in delete_file (`del STORE[fid]`, views.py:18) and rename_file (`f["name"] = ...`, views.py:27), which are authorized by acl.is_allowed using g.user.

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') takes the identity from the raw client header with no verification.
delete_file calls ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') with the spoofed identity.
is_allowed only checks `action in resource['grants'][user]`, so a spoofed name that matches a grantee passes.
rename_file uses the same is_allowed check with the spoofed g.user.

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is the ACL lookup in acl.py, which trusts the identity it is given. There is no authentication middleware, signature check or proxy-trust check in the two files, and no other files exist in the directory. A missing header gives user None, which is denied unless grants has a None key, so the bypass needs the attacker to know or guess a grantee's name. Whether an upstream proxy strips this header is not visible in the code, so this is a precondition that was not verified.

verdict.guard_found: Only the ACL check (acl.py:4-10), which is enforced correctly: ensure_allowed aborts with 403 at acl.py:10, and is_allowed's result is tested at views.py:25. It trusts the supplied identity. No authentication middleware, signature check or proxy-trust check exists in these two files.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 does take g.user straight from the client header, and the ACL at acl.py:5 only matches that name against grants. Whether an upstream proxy strips and re-sets "X-Session-User-Verified" (the name suggests it is meant to) can't be determined from the two files in the directory, so exploitability is unconfirmed.

verdict_facts.guard_found: ACL check via acl.is_allowed/ensure_allowed (acl.py:5, 9-10) is correctly enforced on both routes (views.py:17 aborts 403; views.py:25 returns 403). Identity comes from a "Verified" header set by trusted upstream middleware per the maintainer's project facts.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace lines are accurate (views.py:11, 17-18, 25-27; acl.py:5), but the finding's only weakness is the unverified assumption that the proxy doesn't set the header at views.py:11. The maintainer states request identity is populated by trusted upstream middleware, and the header name "X-Session-User-Verified" fits that, so a client can't spoof it. The ACL checks at views.py:17 and 25 work correctly, so this isn't a vulnerability in this module.
